Purpose

Permanent, temporary, situational

Disability is not one fixed group of people - it is a condition every one of us moves in and out of, in three registers: permanent, temporary, situational.

Situational: A cracked phone screen in direct sun

  • Permanent
  • Temporary
  • Situational

Most of your audience

Disability is permanent, temporary and situational - which makes it most of your audience, most of the time. Accessible design is not charity for an edge case - it is the curb cut everyone rolls through.

Every case, by register

Permanent

  • Blindness
  • Deafness
  • Dyslexia
  • Low vision
  • A tremor that affects fine control
  • Limited speech

Temporary

  • A concussion, week two
  • Recovering from eye surgery
  • A wrist in a splint
  • Medication that makes text blur
  • A migraine that makes light painful
  • Vertigo that makes motion hard to follow
  • Hearing muffled by an ear infection
  • Speech lost after a procedure

Situational

  • A loud factory floor
  • A bright platform at noon
  • Holding a sleeping child
  • Riding a moving bus
  • A borrowed laptop with no mouse
  • Watching video in a silent waiting room
  • Following directions while carrying groceries
  • An unfamiliar kiosk with a queue behind you
  • A weak connection on a rural route
  • A cracked phone screen in direct sun

Press the cube to turn it to another case. Each one is somebody who needs the page to work, some for a lifetime and some for an afternoon.

Challenge

Somebody else’s focus ring

When you move through a page with a keyboard, a ring appears around the thing you are on - a button, a link, a box to type in. That ring is the focus indicator. It is how you know where you are, the same way a cursor shows where you are typing. For everyone who navigates this way - by need or by preference - the ring is not a detail. It is their place on the page, and losing it for even a second means being lost.

Here is the strange part: the people who live by that ring have never once been asked about it. On every site on the internet, the ring is the developer’s choice - their color, their width, their taste, coded in and shipped. Every search you run, every form you file: somebody else’s focus ring. It has no personality because it was never yours.

With this system, that ends - we take those people into account, and we hand the choice over.

Solution

One rule, three tokens

The idea came in August 2026 while I was reading the documentation of a federal design system: people should pick the focus style that works best for them. Focus already lived in three tokens there, so a switch the reader controls cost almost nothing to build.

It went into that system’s accessibility page as the sixth of its guarantees, written into its documentation so a team inherits them by using the components.

Every component draws its focus ring from three tokens: ring color, width and gap. Picking a style sets one attribute on the page root, and that attribute rewrites the three tokens for every element at once.

The header, the footer and every control on this page redraw their rings from those tokens. The choice is saved in the browser, so it holds after a reload and on the next page.

In the AODS documentation the chooser runs as a page template: three styles on the same three tokens.

Rules

Every ring clears 3:1

A ring that fades into its background helps nobody. WCAG 2.2 asks for a visible focus indicator (2.4.7) at 3:1 against what sits beside it (1.4.11), so I measured every style on every ground a ring can land on. Where a style fell short, I added a keyline and kept the style.

Detail

The criteria it answers

Each claim, the criterion it answers and the test behind it.
WCAG 2.2 criterionWhat the page and the system doHow it was measured
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA)Every ring clears 3:1 against the ground beside it, with keylines where a band falls shortRing, keyline and band colors against each of the five grounds, by the WCAG luminance formula
2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA)Every control shows a ring in all four styles, the cube includedA full Tab walk in each style, with the cube’s ring checked by pixel
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, Minimum (AA, new in 2.2)The sticky header and the phone bar never cover the focused controlEach focus stop hit-tested against the header and bar at 1280 and 390
2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA)Each style has a band at least 2 px thick at 3:1 against the unfocused stateThe thinnest band that carries 3:1, per style and ground
2.4.3 Focus Order (A)Reading order, visual order and Tab order match at every widthTab walk at 390, 768 and 1280, checked top to bottom
2.5.8 Target Size, Minimum (AA, new in 2.2)Every control is at least 24 px, and the Try it controls are 44 pxMeasured bounding boxes
2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA)Under reduced motion the cube changes its face without turningTransition time with reduced motion on
4.1.3 Status Messages (AA)A new style and each cube face are announced without moving focusPolite live regions, read after each change
